L2: # Clinical Trials
L3: ### Welcome to a resource for information on current research trials in veterinary oncology.
L4: 
L5: Pet owners often ask us if we are aware of any CLINICAL TRIALS that may be available to their cat or dog who has been diagnosed with cancer. While there certainly are a number of studies occurring around the world, participation in a clinical trial can often be difficult, especially if the trial is going on in a hospital or clinic far away from your home.
L6: Each clinical trial has very specific qualifications for participation that include everything from the breed and age of the participant to the life expectancy, weight and of course the type of cancer. Each study is very particular in its criteria for participation. Something else to take into consideration is that clinical trials are NOT always free.
L7: There may be fees to participate because grants may only cover a certain portion of the trial, and you may have to travel a long way to participate for several weeks or months perhaps.
L8: The following links represent an organized effort to provide general practitioners and their pet owners access to information to trials being conducted across the United States and, in some cases, in other countries.

L92: ## Clinical Research Trial Overview
L93: Clinical trials may involve novel diagnostic methods or therapies including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical procedures, hypo- or hyperthermia, immunotherapy and photodynamic therapy, among others. While most clinical research trials are conducted at colleges of veterinary medicine, a growing number of specialty referral practices are participating in clinical research.
L94: For some trials, all visits must occur at the trials institution or practice, but for others there are tests or procedures that could be performed at the general practice.
L95: When discussing the possibility of participating in a clinical trial with pet owners, it is helpful to share that although “experimental,” or “investigational,” the safety and efficacy of new therapies and procedures have often been evaluated first in laboratory animals as well as normal dogs or cats, and the therapy is considered to be of potential benefit to the patient.
L96: 
L97: 【42†Image: Dr. Sarah Sheafor】
L98: ### Reminder for veterinarians managing pets enrolled in clinical trials
L99: Adherence to the treatment protocol is of vital importance to ensure that the protocol is followed as planned, such that the results are both reliable and meaningful. Any deviation in the pet’s health or management (including medications and supplements) must be reported to the trials institution. For most trials, owners are asked to agree to a necropsy in the event of the death of their pet. Pet owners also may appreciate the translational value of the research in which their pet may be participating.
L100: Many naturally-occurring cancers in pet animals closely resemble human cancer and provide meaningful systems for cancer research to benefit both man and animals.
L101: The clinical trials listed on this website are not run under the auspices of the Veterinary Cancer Society. Clinical trials are performed in order to assess the toxicity and/or efficacy of a certain treatment protocol. While the hope is that the investigators will find a less toxic or more effective treatment for cancer, there are no guarantees regarding the outcome of any trials listed on clinical searchable database found on this site.

L1: # Clinical Trials
L2: 
L3: The medical and surgical diagnostic tests and treatments of animals are similar to those in human medicine. In order to advance knowledge, researchers and clinicians at the College of Veterinary Medicine perform studies that investigate new diagnostics and treatments. These discoveries can often be applied to medicine across all species.
L4: Most clinical trials are based on preliminary laboratory research data that indicate that the new approach is better than what is already available. Benefits to patients in clinical trials include the potential for life-saving therapy when other treatments have failed, lower-cost treatment or diagnostic options, and the advancement of knowledge that will help future patients. Clinical trials are only performed with informed owner consent.
L5: The benefits, risks, and requirements of enrolling in a specific clinical trial is discussed with every client to determine whether participation is the right choice for that patient.
L6: Clinical trials are through one of the Teaching Hospital’s specialty services, typically the Oncology Service, in conjunction with research faculty at the College of Veterinary Medicine.

L221: ## Improving care through clinical trials
L222: 
L223: Clinical trials help doctors in the medical and veterinary fields discover new ways to improve the detection, diagnosis, ​and treatment of illnesses, all while enhancing the quality of care each patient receives. Clinical trials are critical to our groundbreaking research, may provide access to cutting-edge care, and result in discoveries that help people and animals in the future, all while providing your pet with the highest level of personalized care.
L224: 
L225: biotech
L226: ### Participate in a clinical trial
L227: 
L228: When your pet participates in a clinical trial, they help our veterinarians discover disease prevention methods and find new ways to improve detection, diagnosis, and treatment of animal illnesses.

L238: ## Frequently asked questions
L239: ### Why should my pet participate?+
L240: Clinical trials help us evaluate new diagnostics, treatments, or devices to better understand their safety and how well they work. We carefully design studies with strict ethical oversight and ensure you understand the trial’s purpose and any risks. Clinical trials often offer benefits, including access to cutting-edge treatments or financial incentives. All pets enrolled in clinical trials receive unparalleled care from their veterinary team, just like all other VHS patients.
L241: ### What should I expect during a clinical trial?+
L242: When you inquire about a clinical trial, the clinical trial team will review your pet’s medical history. If they appear to be a good fit, you may be contacted to move to the screening step, which may include a review of your veterinarian’s records and an in-person visit. You will have time to review the client informed consent documents and ask questions related to participation in the trial. You will also be presented with alternatives to participating in the clinical trial.
L243: You will learn about the study requirements, including any treatments and follow-up visits that are required. You can decide not to enroll in the trial or withdraw at any time without any negative impact on the care you and your pet will receive.
L244: ### Are clinical trials safe?+
L245: 
L246: All clinical trials undergo extensive review before starting, including review of any potential risks. Just as many aspects of veterinary care carry inherent risks or potential side effects, clinical trials may also have these. The care team will discuss any potential risks with you prior to enrollment.
L247: ### Does it cost anything to participate in a clinical trial?+
L248: 
L249: There may be some associated costs to establish a diagnosis before clinical trial enrollment. Each study will have different associated costs and this will be outlined in the client informed consent document.
L250: 
L251: ### How many visits are required and how long does a trial last?+
L252: 
L253: This is variable depending on the study, ranging from a single visit to lifelong follow-up.
L254: ### How do I know if my pet qualifies for a clinical trial?+
L255: 
L256: Enrollment criteria are established for each clinical trial and may include factors such as size, breed, age, or diagnosis. These will vary for each clinical trial. Please inquire for an individual clinical trial to see if your pet may qualify.
L257: ### Will my primary veterinary be updated if I enroll my pet in a clinical trial?+
L258: 
L259: Yes, your care team will send updates to your veterinarian regarding the care your pet receives as a part of the clinical trial.
